title: A price tag on every door
allegory: A Q-value is like a price tag on every door out of a room, telling you how much treasure you will collect on average if you go through that door now and then carry on with your usual habits.
map: one specific door you could take
the tag: treasure collected if you take this door, then follow your usual habits
Q_π(s, a): expected return from a now, then policy π
the room's own value: the tag on the door you'd normally take
picking the door with the biggest tag
greedy improvement: π′(s) = argmax_a Q(s, a)

cap.1: You're in a room with three doors. Knowing 'this room is a good place to be' doesn't tell you which door to take. You need a score for each door.
cap.2: The state value V(s) scores where you are. To choose, you need a score per action: Q(s, a), the value of taking action a here. Then choosing is easy: take the biggest.
cap.3: V_π(s) averages over the policy's own action, so ranking alternatives needs a model of the dynamics. Q_π(s, a) conditions on the first action, which makes greedy selection model-free.

cap.1: Hang a price tag on every door: the treasure you'll collect on average if you take it now, then carry on with your usual habits. Pick the biggest.
cap.2: Q_π(s, a) is the expected return from taking action a in state s and following policy π afterwards. 'Afterwards' matters: the tag assumes your usual habits from the next room on.
cap.3: Q_π(s, a) = E[Σₖ γᵏ r_{t+k+1} | s_t = s, a_t = a, then π]. Only the first action is free; every later one comes from π, which is why Q is defined relative to a policy.

cap.1: A door's tag is the treasure right behind it, plus the value of the room it leads to, shaved a little because later treasure counts slightly less.
cap.2: Q_π(s, a) = E[r + γ·V_π(s′)]: immediate reward plus the discounted value of wherever you land. And V_π(s) is just the tag on the door your policy would pick: V_π(s) = Q_π(s, π(s)).
cap.3: Bellman: Q_π(s, a) = Σ_{s′} T(s′|s, a)[R(s, a, s′) + γ V_π(s′)], with V_π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Q_π(s, a). The advantage A = Q − V says how much better a door is than your habit.

chapters.name: Read the table
chapters.title: a Q-table: the greedy move is the biggest number in each row

cap.1: Write every tag into a table: one row per room, one column per door. Your best move in any room is just the biggest number in its row.
cap.2: A tabular Q is a (num_states, num_actions) array, and the greedy policy is Q.argmax(axis=1). Note the −9.8: stepping off the cliff edge, which a good table learns to avoid.
cap.3: Policy improvement: π′(s) = argmax_a Q_π(s, a) is never worse than π in any state (the policy improvement theorem). Alternate evaluation and improvement and you reach an optimal policy.

chapters.name: The optimist's trap

left.title: Honest tags (SARSA)
lines: tags for how you really play

right.title: Best-case tags (Q-learning)
lines: max of noisy tags runs high

chapters.verdict: Picking the biggest noisy tag picks the luckiest one: expect optimism.

cap.1: Two ways to fill in tags: by how you actually play, wobbles included, or by how you'd play if perfect from now on. The second gets overexcited.
cap.2: SARSA learns Q for the policy it follows; Q-learning bootstraps with max_a Q(s′, a) and learns optimal Q from any data. But a max over noisy estimates picks the luckiest one, so values drift upward.
cap.3: E[max_a Q̂] ≥ max_a E[Q̂] (Jensen), and bootstrapping compounds it. On CliffWalking, where every true return is negative, positive Q entries expose the bias; Double Q-learning decouples selection from evaluation.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Q is what lets an agent act greedily
DQN: a network that outputs Q
Advantage = Q − V drives policy training

cap.1: Tags on doors are how an agent decides. Scaled up, they drive game-playing agents, and as 'advantage' they drive the RL that fine-tunes language models.
cap.2: DQN replaces the table with a network that outputs one Q per action. The advantage Q − V, 'how much better than my habit', is the signal PPO and RLHF use to push a model's choices.
cap.3: Q bridges evaluation and control: argmax for value-based methods (DQN), and A = Q − V as the low-variance weight in policy gradients (actor-critic, PPO), the machinery behind RLHF-style steering.

coda.title: Snack now, or pay the toll for a better room?

params.label: value of the room behind door B

readouts.label: greedy choice
readouts.f: 5 >= -toll + gamma*later ? 'snack door: grab it now' : 'toll door: worth the wait'

readouts.label: γ where they tie
readouts.f: later > 0 && (5 + toll)/later <= 0.99 ? ((5 + toll)/later).toFixed(2) : 'no tie in range'

caption.1: Slide γ, how much you care about later. Low γ: grab the snack now. High γ: pay the toll for the better room. The tags change, not the doors.
caption.2: Q(snack) = 5 + γ·0 and Q(toll) = −toll + γ·(room value). Greedy picks the bigger Q. Watch Q(toll) − Q(snack) cross zero exactly where γ = (5 + toll) / room value.
caption.3: Q depends on the discount and on what follows, not only on the immediate reward. Here the downstream values are fixed; in general they depend on π, which is why Q is always Q_π.

where_else: DQN: a neural network that outputs one Q-value per action, the Q-table generalised
Advantage, A = Q − V, which weights the updates in actor-critic methods, PPO and RLHF
Tree search: MCTS keeps a running value estimate for each move from each node

hamming.what: The expected total reward from taking one specific action in a state and then following your policy.
hamming.when: Whenever an agent must choose between actions without a model of the world, from tabular Q-learning to DQN.
hamming.why: Scoring each action directly turns choosing into 'take the biggest', and its gap from V (the advantage) is the signal that drives policy training.

object.title: The Q-table skyline
object.subtitle: One tower per room and door: the tallest tower in each row is the move a greedy agent makes.

cap.1: Five rooms along a corridor, three doors each. A tower's height is that door's price tag: treasure at the far end, discounted by distance.
cap.2: A tabular Q for a corridor with +10 on reaching the goal: rows are states, columns are actions, height is Q*(s, a) / 5.
cap.3: Q*(s, right) = 10γ^(4−s); stay and left cost one or two extra discounted steps: 10γ^(5−s) and 10γ^(6−s).

cap.1: In every row the 'right' tower is tallest. That is the greedy policy, read straight off the skyline.
cap.2: Greedy policy = argmax along each row. No model of the corridor is needed: the table already contains the lookahead.
cap.3: π(s) = argmax_a Q(s, a); for Q* this is an optimal policy.

cap.1: Care about the future almost fully and the towers level out: far rooms look nearly as good as near ones.
cap.2: γ near 1 makes distant reward count almost fully, so Q barely decays along the corridor.
cap.3: As γ → 1, Q*(s, a) → 10 for every action that still reaches the goal: the ranking survives but the gaps shrink.

cap.1: Now care little about later: the far rooms' towers collapse. Only doors near the treasure look valuable.
cap.2: A small γ discounts the goal heavily, so Q in far states is tiny: that is why long tasks need γ near 1.
cap.3: Q*(0, right) = 10γ⁴, which at γ = 0.4 is 0.256: a weak signal from a goal five steps away.

cap.1: From above, the right-hand column is the ridge. The advantage is how far a tower sits above or below the room's usual choice.
cap.2: V(s) is the tower the policy picks; A(s, a) = Q(s, a) − V(s) is zero for the greedy door and negative for the others.
cap.3: Under the optimal policy A*(s, a) ≤ 0, with equality at the argmax: the quantity actor-critic methods estimate to weight policy gradients.

predict.q: Q(s, left) = 2, Q(s, right) = 7, Q(s, up) = 4. What does a greedy agent do?

options.t: Go up: the middle value is safest

predict.why: Greedy means take the biggest Q in the current state.

predict.q: Your policy always goes up from s, and Q(s, up) = 4. What is V(s) under that policy?

options.t: The average of all three doors

predict.why: V_π(s) is the tag on the door π actually takes: V_π(s) = Q_π(s, π(s)).

predict.q: On CliffWalking with γ = 1 every true return is negative, yet your Q-learning table shows positive numbers. Why?

options.t: A max over noisy estimates is biased upward
The reward function has a bug
The learning rate is too low

predict.why: The max picks whichever estimate got lucky, and bootstrapping recycles that optimism through the table.
